title: Editing a file in the terminal
summary: Open a file, change it, save it and quit, without leaving the terminal: nano or vi, your choice.

text: On a server there is no mouse and no window: you edit files right in the terminal.
- nano is simple: what you type goes into the file. vi is everywhere, even on the smallest systems.
- The file doesn't exist yet? It's created when you save.
- bashou config editor picks the one your hints and this lesson show.
In nano you type straight into the file. The keys at the bottom are shortcuts: ^ means Ctrl.
- Ctrl+O saves (Enter confirms the name), Ctrl+X quits. With unsaved changes it asks "Save modified buffer?": Y saves, N drops them.
- Ctrl+W searches (newer nano shows it as ^F; both work), Ctrl+K cuts a whole line, Ctrl+U pastes it back.
vi has two modes. It opens in normal mode, where keys are commands, not text.
- i switches to insert mode: now you type text. Esc goes back to normal mode.
- In normal mode, : starts a command: :w saves, :q quits, but refuses if you have unsaved changes: then :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and drops them.
- Lost? Press Esc twice: you're back in normal mode.

text: A few normal-mode keys cover most edits.
- /word searches, n jumps to the next match.
- dd deletes the line under the cursor, x one character, u undoes the last change.
0 goes to the start of the line, $ to the end.
Errors often give a line number. Open the file right on that line with +N.
